en: The Abhidharmadīpa, together with its commentary, the Vibhāṣāprabhāvṛtti. First Chapter.

First Chapter. Having prostrated before the Buddha, who revealed to humans and gods the path that brings about the pacification of the causes of suffering—the Knower of the True Path—I shall compose this treatise, the *Abhidharmadīpa*. [1]
If the *sattva* and other guṇas were unchanging, it would follow that there is no manifestation;
furthermore, because the *prakṛti* is non-different from them, it would undergo modification through their modification. [2]
Karma does not exist because it has been relinquished by its own nature; nor do the stains consist of a cognizable or manifest self-nature.
In the first case, there would be an absence of liberation; in the second case, there would be other afflictions as well. [3]
The aggregate of form consists of the ten bases and elements beginning with the eye; the three aggregates designated as "dharmas" consist of non-informative matter and the three eternal factors.
The other seven consciousness-elements are also designated as "mind.
For an *āyatana* is defined as a door of arrival (*āyadvāra*), while a *dhātu* is defined as a lineage (*gotra*). [5]

The Sage taught the twelve bases (āyatana) because they are conducive to yoga and its form, and he taught the eighteen elements (dhātu) for the sake of abandoning the notion of a single unity regarding the intellect and so forth. [6]
Because the six [consciousnesses] are mutually dependent, that which is their cause is the mind (manas).
Because it serves as the basis for the existence of both the material and the immaterial, the five [sense-consciousnesses] are designated as "material. [7]
The inclusion of the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements within their own selves is taught;
likewise, the equality of mind and mental factors is due to their being eternally inseparable from their own selves. [8]

One who is proficient in the method of the treatise should state that those [dharmas] mentioned by other names in other sūtras are included within these very [categories], having considered their own specific characteristics with the intellect. [9]

The mutual inclusion of the aggregates and so forth should be understood according to their respective natures; there is no inclusion of eternal things within the aggregates, because they do not fall into the time-periods (adhvan) and for other such reasons. [10]
The inclusion of even the eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma should be understood as occurring precisely within these entries, because they lead one to enter the true path. [11]
The measure of the *dharmaskandha*, however, is the teaching of each [truth] and so forth individually;
its true nature, moreover, is held by some to be speech, while others maintain it is even the name. [12]
The six fundamental elements are considered the basis for the designation of "sentient being"; since it is said that through their differentiation, conceit (*asminmāna*) ceases in this regard. [13]
Because it is nourished by the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), consciousness should indeed be understood as being afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) when it serves as the basis for birth.
The element of space (*khadhātu*) is distinct from [mere] space, because it is included within the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*). [14]

Space is indeed the cause proximate to the element of space; these [elements] are the causes of the primary elements (bhūta), those [elements] are the cause of derived form (rūpa) born from them, and this [derived form] is the cause of the mind (cetas). [15]

That which functions as direct perception, that which apprehends even what has not yet been reached, that which reaches objects further away than others, and that which is more proficient than the rest; [16]
In the commentary titled *Vimāṣāprabhā* on the *Abhidharmadīpa*, this is the second chapter of the first section.
In the third chapter of the first book:
"The first category consists of those that are demonstrable; the ten material elements are characterized by resistance."
With the exception of visible form and sound, those very same [factors] are considered to be indeterminate. [17]

The remaining ones here are all of three kinds; in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there are fourteen, excluding the elements of taste and odor along with their respective consciousnesses, and the final three.
The last three are both with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and without-outflows (*anāsrava*); the remaining ones are only with-outflows.
The first five have an object (*sālambana*); the [last] three are of three kinds, including those that are metaphorical (*sopacāra*). [19]

Those whose own objects are qualities free from conceptual construction do not involve memory or discernment; thus, the first [type of mental application] belongs to the level of the mind and consists of memory, while the second is discerning wisdom (*dhī*). [20]

In the desire realm, the fivefold group of consciousnesses is accompanied by one type of conceptualization; other than those, they are accompanied by three. In the first dhyāna, that which is not in meditative equipoise is likewise.
By two [faculties], it is undisturbed; by one, it has its basis in the eye, ear, and skin;
by two, it is disturbed above that; and by one alone, it is concentrated. [22]
For one whose seeds of merit have been severed,
there is no wholesome consciousness with conceptualization, except for that which pertains to rebirth. [23]
For a fool who is free from passion for sense-objects and whose nature is not subject to loss, there is no unwholesome state of either kind; nor is there any superior defiled state for a noble one.
Nothing that is non-afflicted and neutral (akliṣṭāvyākṛta) can have a higher level as its object of conceptualization;
nor does anything afflicted or conceptualizing have a lower level as its sphere of activity.
In three ways, for a noble one who possesses passion and is virtuous, there are two types [of cognition] in the [first] body;
however, in the second [body] and those following, there is neither the virtuous nor the afflicted that perceives [the objects].
Due to prior application, the proximity of the factors, and the homogeneity of the continuum, memory arises in the mind with respect to an object previously experienced by consciousness. [27]
Due to the opposite of this—namely, dullness and being overwhelmed by the disease of the afflictions—forgetfulness arises regarding things previously known. [28]

That which has been seen by a mind of two, three, four, or five types is remembered by that same mind or by others; however, in the case of the destruction of the vision of obstacles, one does not remember what was seen by another.
However, that which is experienced by one among the five consciousnesses is also remembered by another, and indeed by the others as well. [30]
That mind which has experienced two neutral [states], such as the twelve [mental factors] here,
is remembered by eight [factors] alone, because of the cessation of the formless and the formed. [31]

But that which is remembered through the obscured-unwholesome and the wholesome states pertaining to the realms of form and formlessness respectively—excluding the two types of neutral states pertaining to the desire realm—is remembered by means of ten [mental applications]. [32]
In the realm of form (rūpa), that which has been seen by the non-obscured neutral [mind] is remembered again by other [minds], excluding the neutral minds of the formless realm (ārūpya). [33]
The cognition of the neutral states of the formless realm is known by nine [minds];
that [cognition] of the desire realm, excluding the two neutral states, as well as the obscured-unspecified state of the form realm.
The seven [elements] called mind have an object; the one called mental factors is associated.
Those that are formless, together with sound, are non-appropriated; nine are of two kinds. [35]
The tangible is of two kinds: the elements (dharmas) together with their derivatives, which are nine; these ten are possessed of parts, material, and they alone are aggregated. [36]
Visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility are considered to consist of that which cuts and that which is cut;
they are also the burners and the weighed, or else they are the burned and the weighed.
The five material sense-faculties consist of both maturation and accumulation;
the immaterial [faculties] are not accumulative; the remaining [factors] are of three kinds; and sound is of two kinds. [38]
The eye and its perception may be attained either separately or together.
The twelve internal bases are to be known, along with the six external ones consisting of the objects. [39]
The last three are of three kinds; the remaining ones are abandoned through the path of cultivation.
There is no form to be abandoned by seeing, nor is there any that is non-afflicted or non-conceptual.
That which is called "dharma" is exclusively homogeneous; however, the remaining [elements] are known to be of both kinds.
That which is homogeneous is considered such because it participates in its own activity within the state of homogeneity.
The eye and a portion of the sphere of phenomena (dharmadhātu) are said to be vision in nine ways;
the wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses is not vision, because it lacks investigative judgment. [42]

Just as the eye perceives visible objects during nights with clouds or without clouds, so too do those in training and those beyond training perceive with afflicted and unafflicted vision respectively. [43]
In the Abhidharmadīpa, in the commentary known as the Vibhāṣāprabhā, this is the third quarter of the first chapter.
The fourth quarter of the first chapter:
The eye sees; consciousness cognizes its own object.
Because one is the act of looking and the other is the act of apprehension, there is a very great distinction between the two. [44]
The effect of the eye is consciousness, whether it arises from one eye or from both;
the mind, the eye, and the ear do not reach their objects, whereas the other three do so otherwise.
Those [cognitions] that grasp what is not in contact are established because they grasp objects both distant and near;
if it is argued that this is like the light of a lamp and so forth, we say no, because that light arises simultaneously [with its source].
If it is argued that there would be the consequence of [the self] being attached to all objects, we say no, because of the observation of magnets and the like.
If it is argued that there is no fault because of its omnipresence, we say no, because that is illogical, as in the case of sesame oil. [47]
For above the eye there is neither body nor form, nor is there a mind born of the sense-organ;
however, the object of the eye is for consciousness, and both of these are entirely for the body. [48]
Above the ear there is no body, no sound, and no mind of one's own;
yet there is the resonance of consciousness, and those two [body and sound] are present everywhere within the body.
For three [realms], all three [faculties] are their own; for the body, consciousness is also [of] the lower [realm].
The mind, however, is indeterminate; the manifold forms of the yogi have been demonstrated.

Those aggregates which are designated as "clinging" (upādāna) should be known as exclusively with-outflows (sāsrava), because they perform the function of assisting those [outflows] and so forth. [51]
Terms such as "time-period" (*adhvan*) and so forth are synonyms for the aggregates (*skandha*); terms such as "phenomenon" (*dharma*) and so forth refer to existing entities (*vastu*).
However, those which are designated as "with-outflows" (*sāsrava*) are spoken of by the names of "suffering" (*duḥkha*) and the rest. [52]

Because the effects that have as their object the self-nature [of consciousness] are one, they belong to a single element; thus, although there is a twofold division of the eyes and so forth, their arising is dual due to the threefold nature of their activity. [53]
Due to its unique distinction, its sovereignty, and its internal nature,
consciousness is differentiated by those [factors], even though they are not the sole cause. [54]

Because it is eternal and wholesome, Nirvana is truly a substantial entity; since it is a substance consisting of the core essence, the single dharma called "Nirvana" is considered to possess substantial reality.
The first stainless mind is called the "moment" (kṣaṇa) due to its rarity; because of that wondrous moment, these latter three are termed "momentary" (kṣaṇika). [56]

The nose, the tongue, and the body—these three are equal in that they grasp objects of their own level; the support for the last one is past, as is the support for the five together with those [objects].
Indeed, by relying on either the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) or the four meditative supports (*niśraya*),
the visual element (*cakṣurdhātu*) is ceased through the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*).
However, by relying on the *anāgamya* stage, the odor-element (*gandhadhātu*) ceases; or else, the mind-element (*manodhātu*) ceases by relying on the *anāgamya* or the seven supports. [59]

The preliminary stage (*anāgamya*) and likewise the first [dhyāna], which is designated as eye-consciousness, should be explained according to their respective application, due to the manifold nature of the *dharmadhātu*. [60]
For by thoroughly understanding the eye-element as belonging to the realm of form, an ordinary person attains detachment from the entire realm consisting of form. [61]
Therefore, from that element, he abandons thirty-one latent dispositions;
yet at that time, he does not eliminate any of the fetters whatsoever.
When he attains detachment from form, he abandons three underlying tendencies; at that time, the noble one completely exhausts the fetter of "nothingness."
But by thoroughly understanding the element of eye-consciousness, and that very [element],
one necessarily comes to understand it and becomes detached from the Brahma-world.

But at that time, that ordinary person (pṛthagjana), while fully understanding the element of odor and what is called the element of taste, does not completely exhaust any of the fetters (saṃyojana). [65]
He attains detachment from sensual desires and certainly abandons even the underlying tendencies;
at that time, he casts off the thirty-six fetters along with the three bonds.
The Noble One, however, effects detachment from the realm of desire; he fully understands four latent dispositions and also eradicates three.
Fully understanding the mind-element, one becomes detached from the formless realms;
one abandons three underlying tendencies and likewise fully masters the triad.
Indeed, fully understanding that very joy, he abandons it;
he attains detachment from the Ābhāsvara realm, yet he does not destroy the outflows (āsravas).
Fully understanding that pleasure, the yogi abandons it both here and in this world;
he attains detachment from the Śubhakṛtsna realm, yet he does not destroy the afflictions.
The five qualities are cognizable by two [senses]; all causes are both perishable and imperishable.
Apart from the meaning of the *dharmadhātu*, they are external to the six [objects], not consisting of the sense faculties. [71]
In the *Abhidharmadīpa-vibhāṣā-prabhā-vṛtti*, the first chapter;
the second chapter;
the first section.
The factors, beginning with the etymological definitions (nirvacana), will be briefly explained in relation to the entire twenty-two-fold chapter on the faculties (indriya). [72]
By name there are twenty-two, but by substance they are seventeen; because the two [faculties] are not other than the nine [faculties] beginning with pleasure, which constitute three triads. [73]

Because the characteristics of a real entity (sallakṣaṇa) do not exist in that name, yet the name possesses its own meaningful referent; thus, even though the three [categories] function as groups, others will still seek the meaning [of the name]. [74]
Because they are the cause of distinguished cognition and because of their specific predominance,
the two [faculties of sight and hearing] are superior to the body-faculty,
just as the faculties of smell and so forth are superior to it. [75]
The wise designate the object of the senses as that which has sovereignty as its purpose;
this applies to the manifestation of their own objects for five [senses], and to two objects for four [of those five]. [76]
Others know its nature as being the perception of its own object and so forth; others who consider themselves wise say it exists only in the cognition of its own object. [77]
The sequence is established because of the arising of afflictions, the attainment of qualities such as faith, and the purity resulting from the fruit, the defilements, and the accumulations. [78]
Those by which there is the designation of "sentient beings," the diversity of sentient beings, their maintenance, and the arising of afflictions.
The means to the path and the attainment of the fruit are considered their faculty-nature.
There are fourteen [faculties] because they are the basis for contact, its arising, its support, and its enjoyment;
the other eight are faculties because they are the causes of heaven and liberation. [80]
The Sage did not declare desire to be a faculty because it is a constituent part of vigor; nor contact, because it merely augments feeling; nor perception, because it is overcome by wisdom. [81]
Regarding faith and the other faculties, as well as the [five] knowledges, the fault lies in their purification or the arising of defilement;
because of its predominance, mental attention (manaskāra) is not designated as a faculty. [82]
Because it conforms to expectation, resolve (*adhimokṣa*) is also not a faculty;
because of the doubt regarding the production of a fruit at another time, volition (*cetanā*) is not one either. [83]
Nor is this heedfulness due to vigor, nor is it shame because of the restraint of audacity; nor is it equanimity, nor even non-attachment, because of being overwhelmed by vigor and faith. [84]

Pliancy is not [an affliction] because of its intensity; nor are the outflows [afflictions] because they are censurable. Birth and the other [links of dependent origination] are not [afflictions] because they exist for the sake of another; and Nirvana is not [an affliction] because it is devoid of activity. [85]
Bodily affliction is suffering, while mental distress is sorrow;
pleasure and gladness are happiness, whether physical or mental.
Due to its excellence, mental pleasure is in some instances designated as "sukha" (bliss). [87ab]
In the six stages, the faculties such as the "dustless" (nīrajaska) and so forth are to be known; the others, however, are to be seen as stainless faculties belonging to the nine stages. [88]
The three mental sensations associated with dissatisfaction (*daurmanasya*) are to be abandoned by two [paths]; the three mental sensations are of three kinds;
nine are to be abandoned by cultivation (*abhyāsa*).
The five are of two kinds, but not three. [89]
In the desire realm, two types of maturation are obtained through those arising in succession;
by others, six, seven, or eight; but in the form realm, six; while in the last [the formless realm], only the life-faculty. [90]
In the death state, three are ceased; in the intermediate state, eight;
and in the desire realm, ten, eight, nine, four, or five wholesome states are ceased. [91]
The first quarter of the second chapter in the *Abhidharmadīpa-vibhāṣāprabhā-vṛtti*.
In the second chapter, second section:

the attainment of the beginning and the end is by nine; that of the two middles is by seven and eight; and the attainment of the final fruit is by eleven, through the abandonment [of defilements]. [92]
The thorough knowledge of one's own element occurs by way of viewing its own discordant factors. [93ab]

The full comprehension of the desire realm is generally held to be by means of seven [knowledges]; however, it is said to be by means of eight things when both those with stains and those without stains are considered.
The full comprehension of the form realm is held to be by means of ten faculties;
the full comprehension of the final realm is said to be by means of eleven.
All sentient beings dwelling in the three realms are endowed with equanimity, life-force, and the mind;
those in the desire realm possess skin, femininity, and the male organs, while those in the form realm possess the eye and other faculties.

Indeed, one who possesses desire is [afflicted] by suffering; one who possesses passion for that [desire] is dejected; but one born in the higher realms is [afflicted] by pleasure. The Noble One is likewise [afflicted] by the "good" and those born below by the "unpleasant. [97]
Through affection, he produces [offerings] with his arms and lower body; by means of wholesome [deeds], he is rooted in the wholesome.
Those on the path of liberation are those in training (śaikṣa); the Arhat is one beyond training (aśaikṣa), proceeding upon his own path. [98]
One who possesses equanimity or life-faculty is necessarily endowed with three;
one who possesses bodily pleasure or the eye-faculty is endowed with four; and one who possesses the mind-faculty is endowed with five. [99]
One endowed with the female faculty and so forth is possessed of eight; one who experiences suffering is joined with seven;
one possessing the last two [faculties] has eleven; and one possessing the first seven has six.
Those born in the three continents or in the hells, even those fixed in falsehood, are endowed with nineteen or, at minimum, eight [of these faculties]. [101]
Those in the intermediate state, hungry ghosts, animals, and those who follow through faith are endowed with either thirteen or nineteen [faculties]. [102]
Those who are fixed in rightness and those who are liberated through faith are endowed with eleven, or with ten, or with nine faculties. [103]

The Arhats known as those liberated by wisdom (prajñāvimukta), the body-witnesses (kāyasākṣin), and those called both [liberated by wisdom and by mind], possess eleven faculties; or, if they are endowed with eighteen [faculties]. [104]
The gods of the desire realm (kāmadeva), having died, [are reborn] after ten and seven more [days];
they are joined with nineteen [factors] by means of many faculties. [105]
But those born in the two dhyānas possess, at minimum, ten faculties plus five;
the Śubhakṛtsnas are endowed with ten plus four. [106]
For the Bṛhatphala deities are endowed with only the very few thirteen [faculties],
whereas these [deities of the Śuddhāvāsa] are possessed of all sixteen faculties in their entirety. [107]
The formless realms possess eight, ten, and eleven [faculties] respectively; beings, including the gods of the desire realm and the Kurus, are endowed with thirteen.
One who is devoid of virtue (aśubha) is endowed with eight, or with ten—that is, three more—or with the last two, or with very few, up to twenty-one. [109]
An external atom is inseparable from seven substances; in the realm of desire, it is increased by one in the body, and increased by two in the eyes and other sense organs. [110]
In this same way, it should be understood for form as well, excluding the two—smell and taste;
the mind, together with its mental factors, is conditioned by its own specific characteristics.
The second quarter of the second chapter in the *Abhidharmadīpa-vibhāṣāprabhā-vṛtti*.
The third section of the second chapter:
The ten universal mental factors (mahābhūmika) are: discernment, perception, volition, mindfulness, desire, contact, resolve, wisdom, concentration, and attention. [112]
Faith, heedfulness, diligence, serenity, moral shame, dread of blame, the roots, vigor, and non-harming—these are known as the ten wholesome mental factors. [113]

Stiffness, heedlessness, lack of faith, laziness, delusion, and restlessness—these six are present in the defiled mind; however, in the unwholesome mind, there are two: shamelessness and lack of dread. [114]
Deceit, guile, intoxication, anger, harmfulness, envy, malice, subtle crookedness, pride, and avarice— these ten are the ground of the minor afflictions. [115]

Just as a substance such as earth is distinguished by various words through its connection with qualities such as blue, so too is the mind distinguished through its connection with mental factors (caitta). [116]

Just as the diversity between the primary elements (bhūta) and their derivatives (bhautika) is established by their own nature and activity, so too should the distinctness of the mind (citta) and mental factors (caitta) be understood. [117]

Just as a transformation is perceived in water due to its connection with something related to it, so too should the modification of the mind be observed due to its association with that which it comes into contact with. [118]
"Quality," "qualifier," "attribute," "that which occurs in a measure," and likewise "substratum"—words such as these function in dependence upon a primary referent. [119]
Among these, the mind is primary because it grasps the mere object and so forth;
it is also the seed of all activities, as well as of both purity and defilement. [120]
The mind belonging to the desire realm arises together with twelve factors;
it is undefiled and neutral, like the sun with its rays.
Likewise, the mind arises as obscured by eighteen mental states;
however, when accompanied by twenty-two, the mental state is necessarily virtuous. [122]
An unwholesome mind arises together with twenty mental factors;
that which is associated solely with delusion regarding the truths, but one should say it has more when associated with anger and so forth. [123]
Since torpor is possible everywhere, one should specify it wherever it occurs;
and in the same way, one should count regret as an additional factor in some cases. [124]
Impurity, torpor, and remorse do not exist in the realm of form;
furthermore, applied thought and sustained thought do not exist in the intermediate dhyāna, nor above it.
The associated formation is that which possesses fivefold equality;
the dissociated formation is to be understood as that which lacks such equality. [126]
Because there is no existence of distinct [entities], there is no over-extension regarding material things;
and because of the inclusion of "conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskāra*), there is no [over-extension] for space and so forth.
It follows as a logical consequence.
The dissociated formations, beginning with acquisition (prāpti), are thirteen;
their characteristic mark will be stated as being the words of an authoritative person and their own activity. [128]
Acquisition (prāpti), possession (samanviti), attainment (labdhi), the state of possessing dharmas (dharmavattā), and the establishment (vyavasthiti).
And of those consisting of hearing and reflection, as well as of the two meditative attainments.

But for those who possess the impure conditioned wholesome states, their initial acquisition is held to be of three kinds: simultaneous with the [acquisition of the state], prior to it, or subsequent to it. [131]
The defiled and the wholesome are considered to be of three kinds;
likewise, the obscured-unspecified [is of three kinds] for the knowledge and the mind of emanation.
In the initial attainment of Nirvana—which is eternal and distinct from all else—it is held that it is unarisen, present, and at times threefold. [133]
That which is the cause for sentient beings' shared inclination toward a single object is "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā).
The "state of non-perception" (āsaṃjñika) is a karmic maturation (vipāka), consisting of that which cuts off the mind in those who possess perception.

The attainment of the perception of the auspicious is in the final dhyāna; it obstructs the mind because it proceeds from a desire for liberation. It is not attained by an Ārya, but is acquired through preparatory effort.
But that which is called cessation should be understood as belonging to one who desires to abandon [the defilements] born at the peak of existence.
The preparatory application of the noble wholesome [state] is considered to be of two types of feeling and indeterminate.

This state without mind is established through the absence of the fourfold mental consciousness, through scripture, through reasoning, and because of the nature of the mind as being devoid of sensation. [137]
The subsistence of vitality, consciousness, and heat is the basis for the designation of "gati" (destiny/rebirth);
it is accepted as a real entity (dravyataḥ) both on the basis of scripture and through reasoning. [138]
Arising, duration, decay, and destruction—these four are the characteristics of the conditioned.
There are not four [characteristics], because [if there were more], the non-existence of duration and so forth would follow, as their status as causes and so on would be unestablished. [139]
The establishment of decay follows from the loss of power; it is not due to being something else, for that would imply transformation.
The loss of power is established through the destruction of its single causal efficiency. [140]

Since destruction occurs when there is birth, and because it follows from the destruction of substance and activity, as well as from scripture and logical reasoning, destruction too has a cause. [141]

The three— namely, name (nāman) and so forth— are traditionally taught as having their birth dependent upon vocal sounds, performing the function of conveying their own referents, and consisting of designations such as names and the like. [142]

Other things, such as names and so forth, are to be understood as impermanent because they reveal objects that have not been previously attained; for they manifest their objects only through dependence [on other factors]. [143]

A word, while making known its own form as well as suffixes and so forth, certainly causes the meaning to be understood; it is by the wise, through a figurative construction, that it is called [a denoter]. [144]

Because it has the nature of atoms, the oneness of sound is not tenable; identity [with atoms] is impossible because of its resistance, and its establishment is through obstruction and so forth. [145]
No other eternal word known as *sphoṭa* is established apart from sound; nor is any meaning expressed by a word through its sequential occurrence. [146]
A sound is not heard by means of hearing, nor is there any other mode of apprehension for what is heard;
whoever should say otherwise would cause himself to be ridiculed by the wise.
These [qualities] are to be illustrated as appropriate, both determinate and indeterminate;
because of the manifestation of the determinate ones, it is understood that the Buddha is omniscient. [148]

Those called "sentient beings" belong to the realms of desire and form; they are outflowing and indeterminate, as is their maturation. Likewise, acquisitions are of two kinds, according to their similarity.
[In the Abhidharmadīpa-vibhāṣāprabhā-vṛtti, the third quarter of the second chapter.
[The second chapter is completed.
The third chapter.
The fourth quarter:
According to the Sūtra, because there is an absence of calamities known as those affecting sentient beings, there is no [destruction] in the fourth [dhyāna];
[this refers to] the equality of the celestial palace (vimāna).
Since it has been utterly destroyed, how can there be permanence?

After seven destructions by fire and one by water have occurred, and after another seven destructions by water, there is a final series of seven destructions by fire; thereafter comes the destruction by wind.
From the sevenfold group of the Āgneyas, immediately after Pāvanīki,
there is the acquisition of longevity; thus follows the fueling of the Śubhakṛtsna lifespan.

Because they share the same characteristics as the humors such as wind (*vāta*), they are the destroyers of sentient beings; due to this internal correspondence, the destruction of the earth is not considered [to be the same]. [153]
The fourth quarter of the third chapter in the Abhidharmadīpa, in the commentary known as the Vibhāṣāprabhā, is completed.
[The third chapter is completed.]
The Fourth Chapter. The First Section. Of the causes for the rebirth of sentient beings, which bring about both misfortune and prosperity.
It is maintained that karma is the cause of the diversity of the world for those who bring it about. [154]
Action consists of that which is physical, that which is verbal, and that which is mental, known as volition;
these are the causes of the world, not God or other such entities.

Because of its manifold nature, because of its sequential production, and because it would entail the same for other things, there is no dependence on anything else; for the conjunction of austerity [with the self] would involve faults such as the abandonment of one's own thesis. [156]
The power of karmas is awakened by means of ritual injunctions, time, the planets, and so forth; therefore,
the designation of those [factors] as "karma" is employed through a figurative application of the term.
The former are informative and non-informative [action], while volition is mental action.
[The First Pāda of the Fourth Chapter in the Abhidharmadīpa-vibhāṣāprabhā-vṛtti] / The Second Pāda of the Fourth Chapter:
Food in the absence of fire.
Just as a pot that has been fired is properly prepared, so too is the ethical discipline of one whose self is wounded by evil views, deceit, envy, and the like. [159]
Therefore, from the perspective of ultimate truth, monkhood consists in being endowed with both conventional and true vision;
however, through conventionality alone it is a single perfection, and in the absence of both, it is neither in either way.
The primary designation for the Buddha’s teaching refers to knowledge free from afflictions;
it should be understood that the secondary designation applies both to its basis and to its fruit. [161]
Because it is eternal and pure, and because all misfortunes have ceased, Dharma is likewise called Nirvana according to the primary conceptualization. [162]
The noble ones, the qualities of the disciples, and likewise the Saṅgha from the perspective of ultimate truth— whosoever goes for refuge to these three, he goes for refuge to the Triple Gem.
Sexual misconduct is censured by the virtuous because it results in the failure to refrain from what is forbidden in the next world;
false speech is most sinful; and the drinking of intoxicants leads to the loss of memory.
The [discipline] born of desire is obtained from all present [actions], whether they be of two kinds;
however, those consisting of cultivation are obtained from the fundamental [actions] of the three times.
Restraint is taken from all classes of sentient beings by means of its constituent parts and causes;
it is not taken from all the constituent parts of restraint nor from all sentient beings by means of causes.
The acquisition of non-restraint occurs either through action or through formal undertaking;
for other types of non-informative matter, it arises from the excellence of the field, the constituent parts, and so forth. [167]
The abandonment of the restraint pertaining to the desire realm occurs through the renunciation of the precepts and so forth;
some say it also occurs through a downfall, while others say not, because that is inconsistent.
The substance of the cloth perishes through the destruction of its constituent parts by disjunction;
the mention of "destruction" regarding the thread has another meaning, just as it does in cases such as envy, deceit, and the like. [169]

Due to the disappearance of the True Dharma, other [roots of merit] are abandoned; however, those not previously acquired are not lost. Furthermore, the virtue born of dhyāna is abandoned through the transition between stages and through retrogression. [170]
Likewise, noble non-restraint pertaining to the formless realm is lost through the attainment of a fruit, the loss of the faculties, or death;
whereas non-restraint [pertaining to the desire realm] is lost through the acquisition of self-control, death, and so forth. [171]
But the intermediate non-informative action arises through the interruption of the force of the mind and so forth.
That which is called wholesome belonging to the desire realm is destroyed by three causes, such as the cutting off of the roots and so on.

Through the arising of the counteragent, the afflicted [state] belonging to the three realms is abandoned. All [afflictions] are abandoned in the desire realm; in the form realm, twelve; in the formless realm, one, by way of acquisition.
Action that yields a desirable fruit is designated as wholesome (*kuśala*); by the opposite, it is unwholesome (*akuśala*); and other than these, it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). [174]
The first type of merit is included within the realm of desire; non-merit consists of that which is unwholesome in nature.
That which belongs to the higher planes is "imperturbable" (āneñja), because it does not shake with respect to its maturation.

Wholesome (*śubha*) karma is to be experienced as pleasure from the first dhyāna down to the fourth; elsewhere, it is to be experienced as equanimity. However, unwholesome (*pāpaka*) karma is to be experienced as suffering. [176]
Even in the lower realms, there is intermediate karma, because of the attainment of Nirvana even in the final dhyāna,
because of the desire for three simultaneous ripenings, and because of the ripening of the *dhyānāntara* state.
Furthermore, action is of four kinds, distinguished as that to be experienced in the present life and so forth;
by three of these, birth is projected, with the exception of that called "to be experienced in the present life."
Furthermore, all four [types of karma] project [rebirth] everywhere except in hell;
for there is no desirable fruit there, since only the auspicious ripens. [179]

In that regard, an ordinary person who is detached from the two realms of rebirth and has performed actions to be experienced upon rebirth is stable; likewise, a noble one—even if unstable—is so regarding the roots of existence. [180]
When an action is repeatedly practiced with a mind that is either afflicted or fierce,
or when it is performed toward a "good field," its fruit is determined.
Furthermore, due to the excellence of the field and the intention, the fruit ripens immediately;
and in cases such as emerging from cessation, there is the performance of action with immediate temporal results.
One should know that karma which does not arise again in that same plane, and which is fixed as to its maturation, is "fulfilling" (paripūraka) karma; it bears fruit in this very life. [183]
The maturation of wholesome [karma] that is without investigation is exclusively mental feeling;
however, the bodily [feeling] is held to be the maturation of karma to be experienced as suffering.
The impure is black with its maturation; that which is born of form is white with its maturation.
The body (me) is twofold—pure and impure—and that which brings about their abandonment is stainless. [185]

The four paths of seeing constitute the path of vision; the paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) within the realm of desire constitute the path of cultivation through volition. This karma is that which destroys black [karma].

But that volition which exists in the ninth [moment], belonging to the path of immediate succession at the end of each dhyāna, destroys both the black and the black-white karma; however, it is white in the case of the pure (śukla) dhyānas.
All unwholesome karma of body and so forth is considered misconduct (*duścarita*); likewise, the three beginning with covetousness (*abhidhyā*) constitute the threefold mental misconduct. [188]
That which is auspicious, beginning with non-covetousness and so forth, is called the three types of good conduct (*sucarita*).
This consists of two fundamental karmas; the paths are tenfold, both auspicious and inauspicious.
[From the *Abhidharmadīpa-vibhāṣāprabhā-vṛtti*, the second quarter of the fourth chapter;
the third quarter of the fourth chapter:
The six [paths of action] performed are non-informative (*avijñapti*); those consisting of the two doors [of body and speech] are also made into six.
The seven virtuous [mental factors] are to be known as being of two kinds; those that are concentrated are of one kind.
That which is non-informative (avijñapti) in the preliminary stages is the reverse in the subsequent stages;
however, the preliminary effort arises from the three roots, while covetousness and the others are born from the three roots. [191]
The wholesome [actions], along with their preliminary and concluding stages, arise from the three roots of wholesomeness;
the completion of killing, harsh speech, and malice occurs through hatred. [192]
Theft, sexual misconduct with another's wife, and covetousness arise from greed;
false view arises from delusion; it is held that the others arise from all three. [193]
The basis for each of these four should be known in their respective order:
sentient beings, then enjoyments, name-and-form, and name. [194]
Taking life is the intentional killing of another without error.
Taking what is not given is said to be the appropriation of another's property without it being relinquished.

Sexual intercourse with another's wife is sexual misconduct; it is characterized by conceptual construction. False speech is speaking otherwise than the truth regarding a matter one knows, with a malicious intent. [196]
That which is apprehended by the eye, by hearing and so forth, and by the mind,
is respectively called the seen, the heard, the sensed, and the known. [197]
Slanderous speech is talk that causes division; harsh speech is that which is unpleasant; and frivolous chatter is defiled talk such as singing, storytelling, and the like—so say others. [198]
Covetousness is the longing for another's property; ill-will has sentient beings as its object; and false view is the view of nihilism or eternalism, or the view that there is no cause. [199]
Volition is not the path of action; rather, it is by means of those [factors] that existence proceeds, simultaneously with up to eight unwholesome volitions. [200]
By means of the ten wholesome [paths of action], up to half of all [unwholesome paths],
and not by one, eight, or five;
[these include] idle chatter, malice, and harsh speech.
In hell, there are two kinds. [201]
In that very same way, covetousness and likewise false view are considered to exist there;
thus, the triad beginning with covetousness exists in Kuru, as do the two kinds of idle chatter.
The ten unwholesome [paths of action] are acquired elsewhere; the three wholesome ones are acquired everywhere.
Furthermore, those with form—excluding those in the formless realm, the noble ones, and those without perception—acquire seven through attainment.
Excluding the Kurus and the hell-beings, they exist in both ways everywhere else;
all ten [types of action] yield the fruit of maturation, the fruit of outflow, and the sovereign fruit.
Suffering arises from the infliction of pain, shortness of life from killing, and feebleness of vigor from the destruction of vitality; this is the threefold fruit thereof. [205]
An action on the path of immediate retribution possesses five fruits; however, a noble action that is stainless possesses four. Likewise, other wholesome or unwholesome actions are similar.
Other than that, the stainless [dharma] should be known as such; likewise, it is indeterminate with respect to three [types of karma].
Of wholesome [karma], there are four fruits; and for the [fruits] beginning with the wholesome, there are two and three [results] respectively.
For an unwholesome [action], wholesome and other [factors] are respectively two, three, and four;
for an indeterminate [action], those same [factors], beginning with the wholesome, are respectively two, three, and three.
All four [kinds of karma] belong to the past and the present; two belong to the future; three belong to one's own birth; and three belong to a future birth other than one's own. [209]
Four [fruits] belong to one stage, or two or three belong to other stages;
for the learner (śaikṣa), there are three starting from the learner's state, and those same [three] belong to the karma of the non-learner (aśaikṣa).
One, three, and two respectively belong to the [fruits] beginning with that of the learner (śaikṣa) for the last [fruit];
however, for karma to be abandoned by seeing (dṛgheya), there are two, two, and five respectively.
Three, four, and one are remembered as being abandoned by vision and so forth;
however, for that which is to be abandoned by cultivation, two, four, and three are considered to be of three kinds.
Respectively, one, two, three, and four [births] pertain to that karma which is not to be abandoned; one birth is projected by a single [karma], while it is fulfilled by many. [213]
Whether wholesome or unwholesome, whatever past action of one's own body, speech, or mind yields its fruit—that is considered "the state of being the owner of one's own karma. [214]
Conventionally, because the fruit of those actions is seen within the continuum of the aggregates, agency and enjoyership are taught; however, these are denied in the case of an eternal [self].
There is a fourfold set of possibilities regarding whether one possesses ownership of one's own karma (karmasvakatā) and yet that karma does not exist:
the first case applies to one established in the fruit [of the path],
because that karma has been abandoned.
The second [type of person] is one who abides in the fruit of that [path], because of being connected with that karma;
the third is one endowed with both; but the fourth is one who possesses neither. [217]
There may be ownership of karma, yet one will not experience its fruit;
this should be understood as the first state of abiding in that fruit, occurring at the final stage of the fruit. [218]
The second [type of karma] is that whose ripening is certain, because its maturation is not subject to change;
the third is that which possesses both [certainty and changeability]; but the fourth is that which lacks both.
There may be one who is indeed possessed of karma, yet does not experience its fruit;
this is the first case, due to [karma] that has already yielded its ripening, or that which has ceased, or that which is yet to come, and so forth.
The second, however, belongs to one who is devoid of karma that is certain to ripen;
the third belongs to one who is free from both; but the fourth belongs to one who is devoid of both. [221]
Some wise ones say that an action performed improperly is defiled by the primary and secondary afflictions, and is devoid of the characteristics of the training and so forth. [222]
The third quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Abhidharmadīpa*, in the commentary known as the *Vibhāṣāprabhā*.
The Fourth Chapter, Fourth Section:
From what point until when does a bodhisattva become irreversible?
It is from the moment they don the armor of enlightenment, having resolved upon the welfare of the world. [223]
When one who does not go to the states of woe performs the characteristic action, being of noble lineage,
possessing all intact faculties, and devoted to gathering his own assembly.
Then he becomes a male, remembering his past births, eloquent, and endowed with wisdom, vigor, and action; thus he attains manifestation among gods and humans.
For he gathers an ocean of qualities for the Dharma-body over three incalculable eons,
whereas the body that serves as its support is acquired through a hundred eons.
Endowed with the thirty-two marks and radiant with the eighty minor characteristics,
even the minds of enemies are instantly gladdened upon seeing him.
Mount Meru by the wind at the end of an eon, and the abode of Varuṇa by fire.
The vajra is destroyed by the vajra, yet that mind remains unchanging.
That which belongs to the desire realm, born of the sixth [consciousness], is threefold: compassion, faith, and the succession of others.
When a Buddha appears, a man or a woman attains that first mind.
To speak everything, to everyone, at all times, while fulfilling the perfection of generosity,
and not abandoning self-restraint even unto death— this is called the excellence of ethical discipline.

Through the praise of Tiṣya, the perfection of vigor is established; through the diamond-like concentration, that of wisdom is established; and finally, the perfection of all the others is ordained in the knowledge of exhaustion. [231]
The three bases of meritorious action and so forth are the teachings on the means for attaining that;
likewise, there is the fourfold empowerment and the instruction on the seven true dharmas.
The seven yogas, the three aggregates, and the three trainings and so forth have been taught;
likewise, the four perfections have also been proclaimed in the Vinaya.

And the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment have been explicitly taught by the Self-Existent One as the causes for all forms of awakening, categorized as threefold according to their degrees of weakness and so forth.
Therefore, there is no path to enlightenment other than the three baskets (piṭaka) beginning with the Sūtras;
hence, whoever here should speak otherwise would be speaking the words of Māra.
This triad of great incalculable eons (mahāsaṃkhyeya-kalpa) is considered to be a distinct stage called "the incalculable" (asaṃkhya), which stands above ordinary calculation.
The appearance of a Victor occurs during the period of decline, as long as the lifespan is one hundred years;
Pratyekabuddhas appear during both periods [of increase and decline]; and Cakravartin kings appear only during the period of increase.
He does not arise below eighty thousand [yojanas];
his birth there is held to be due to the power of merit. His wheels are made of gold, silver, copper, and iron.

Even when the means of accomplishment are equal, there is a distinction between them due to the difference in the sense organs and so forth, just as there is a difference in the results of giving between two mothers who both seek worldly existence and liberation. [239]
Through the intensity of the cultivation of compassion, as well as through one's own self-awareness and the mind,
the specific excellence of the Guru— who possesses the awareness of others— is likewise established.
The greatness of the Teacher is threefold, arising from the reality of the cause and the result;
for although liberation is equal for all three, they attain the three types of enlightenment.
When the Buddha is present before one, his Buddha-body is manifested;
each individual mark of the Sage is produced from a hundredfold merit.
Just as there are paths of action, so too are the three types of merit and the rest maintained;
for generosity is that by which one gives, depending on the welfare of oneself, others, and so forth.

The actions of body and so forth are that very reality; furthermore, in some cases, it is called "non-informative" (avijñapti) by the Sage because of its predominance, for that indeed has great enjoyment as its fruit.
Some give gifts for the sake of accomplishing their own purpose and that of others;
others do so for the sake of following the conduct of the virtuous, and still others do so for neither purpose. [245]
The excellence of that fruit is traditionally held to arise from the distinction of the giver, the object, and so forth;
thus, through qualities such as faith, the giver bestows [the gift] with acts of respect and the like. [246]
From that, one obtains a fruit endowed with qualities such as being well-honored;
an object perfected by color and other attributes bestows fruits such as physical beauty. [247]
The field is distinguished by the factors known as virtue, suffering, and benefit;
and the mildness and so forth of the action [are distinguished] by the mildness and so forth of the intention and other [factors]. [248]
Giving to one who bestows the Dharma, to a child, to a father, to a mother, to the sick,
to a Bodhisattva, and to one in another existence is immeasurable.
That which is the gift of a Bodhisattva,
as well as that which is the eighth, has been declared by the wise to be superior— that which is given by one Arhat to another Arhat. [250]
When an action has been fully resolved, projected, strengthened by fulfillment and so forth, and is devoid of any counteractive force, it is considered accumulated karma. [251]
And when there is an expectation of the quality of one's own renunciation during the worship of caityas and the like,
there is a fruit even without a recipient, just as in the case of dwelling in loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
The nature of the gift of Dharma has as its sphere names, words, and so forth;
because its nature is indeterminate, it is not like the gift of food and such, which consists of names and the like.
Virtue has been explained as form consisting of the beautiful, according to its various classifications;
however, in the treatise, it is taught as the primary cause for rebirth in heaven.
That which is not defiled by faults such as immorality and the roots of unwholesomeness, and which possesses the factors for the pacification of their opposites, is here called "pure. [255]
But here, merit is concentrated; because it is the cultivation of the mind, it is preeminent for liberation, as has been taught by the All-Seeing One. [256]
In this teaching, the roots of merit are briefly held to be of three kinds: those conducive to merit, those conducive to nirvāṇa, and likewise those conducive to penetration. [257]
Furthermore, writing, sealing, and calculation are characterized by the actions of body and speech;
indeed, numbering should also be understood as having the nature of mental action. [258]
The fourth chapter in the Abhidharmadīpa, with the commentary Vibhāṣāprabhā, is completed.
The Fifth Chapter, First Section: Since the world is inclined toward what ought not to be done and is subject to suffering by virtue of that [ignorance].
I shall now explain those afflictions, such as attachment and so forth, which bind one to existence.

However, those [factors] such as the latent dispositions (anuśaya) and so forth, having acquired general designations through their own names—which arise from specific qualities produced by actions born of their own potential—are thus designated. [260]
Attachment, aversion, delusion, pride, doubt, and wrong views—
these six are declared to be the latent tendencies that obstruct the gateway to the supreme good.
Due to the twofold division of attachment, they are considered seven; due to the divisions of views, they are recorded as ten.
Furthermore, through the distinctions of realms, aspects, and so forth, they should be known as ninety-eight.

Attachment is divided into two types: that which is called attachment to sense-pleasures (*kāmarāga*) and that which is called attachment to existence (*bhavarāga*); this distinction arises because the former generally functions outwardly, while the latter functions inwardly, and so forth. [263]
The view of a self-identity, the two types of grasping at extremes, false view, and the adherence to views and to rules and rituals—these are the five views. [264]
In this context, ten are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering; seven are destroyed by the vision of the cause;
seven are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation; and eight are destroyed by the vision of the path.

Because they take as their objects what is to be abandoned by vision and because they always grasp at aspects, the four—attachment and the others—are to be known as being exhausted by both paths. [266]
Because they arise by the power of each respective eon, views and doubt cease with the destruction of vision;
it is the same regarding form, as well as the formless realm, except for the latent tendency of resistance.
Those [defilements] at the peak of existence which are to be abandoned by patience (kṣānti) are considered to be abandoned only by seeing (dṛg).
However, those which are to be destroyed by knowledge (jñāna) therein, their destruction occurs only through cultivation (abhyāsa).
The view that "I" and "mine" is known as the view of a self-existent body (satkāyadṛṣṭi); the grasping at its annihilation or permanence is considered the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi). [269]
The denial of cause and effect is called false view;
the grasping at inferior things as superior is to be known as the adherence to views.
For that which is called "asceticism and observances" (śīlavrataparāmarśa) consists in taking as a cause that which is not a cause and taking as a path that which is not a path;
since it is a mistaken adherence to a path that leads to suffering, it must indeed be abandoned by one who seeks excellence.

Because the view of a self-identity is severed by the observation of mere phenomena, and because that occurs during the clear realization of suffering, it is therefore to be abandoned by that very vision. [272]
Two [of the perversions] arise from the adherence to views; one arises from the view of a self-identity; and the other half of the remaining [perversion] is designated as a perversion. [273]
Because they function through investigation, superimposition, and error,
these very [views] are called "perversions" (viparyāsa) with respect to vision and cognition. [274]
There are seven types of conceit based on the three [feelings], and nine types of conceit based on the three [realms].
These are further divided into three types each, such as excessive elevation and so forth; thus there is the existence and non-existence of self-exaltation and the like. [275]
Furthermore, the outbursts of anger and the like, as well as unwholesome regret and the desire for non-existence,
do not arise in the noble one due to the absence of their causes.

The establishment of all universal [defilements] arises from both suffering and its origin; this applies to all those born of views to be abandoned by insight, as they abide in the two stations. [277]
Doubt, the five views, ignorance—whether mixed with them or independent—are the seven universal [defilements]. From among these, four are the cause of suffering. [278]
Substantially, there are eleven, but by name they are considered seven;
however, attachment, aversion, and pride function as discerners.
Because they exist in different modes, they simultaneously reach all their own levels; because they take other realms as their objects, those previously mentioned are indeed "all-pervading."
Among those, nine belong to the upper realms; with the exception of the first two views, their co-existent dharmas and all-pervading factors, excluding acquisitions, also belong to them.
Furthermore, ignorance associated with doubt and wrong view, as well as ignorance alone—these six are abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path; they are not seen by the stainless eye.
One abiding on the path attains nirvāṇa only within one's own level;
it does not belong to another level.
That which is another specific object of perception is so because of its state as a cause, due to its being a cause for one another.

There is no passion, because it lacks the cause that is power; no hatred, because there is no offense; no pride, because of extreme tranquility; and no other views, because of the absence of substantial existence. [284]
A universal latent disposition (anuśaya) adheres to its entire sphere;
one that is not universal adheres to its own level by way of its object and to its own category.

Because it is not accepted [as an object] and because it is of a different category, it does not have the higher realms or the Path as its object; however, it has its own associated factors as its object when they are not abandoned, by way of association.
Because these adhere through the analogies of a nurse, clothing, and dirt, and through the manner of birds and aquatic creatures, they are therefore known as "latent tendencies" (*anuśaya*).
Because they persist even in the moments of atoms through various forms such as one's own desired [states] and so forth.
And therefore, the latent dispositions (anuśaya) are considered [to be of two kinds].
The first quarter of the fifth chapter in the *Abhidharmadīpa-vibhāṣāprabhā-vṛtti*.
In the second quarter of the fifth chapter:
The first two views are considered obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) in the desire realm;
however, in the two higher realms, all defilements are likewise obscured-unspecified. [289]

The remaining unwholesome states regarding sensual pleasures are attachment, aversion, and delusion; therefore, there are exactly three roots of the unwholesome due to their connection with five reasons. [290]
The two types of indeterminate states also have three roots equal to those [of the unwholesome]:
ignorance, intellect, and craving; neither doubt, pride, nor views [are roots].

Because it is mobile, because it exists above, and because it is non-pervasive—respectively—and due to a failure to understand the meaning of the Sūtra, the [argument] regarding the impelling of the meditator is not a valid reason. [292]
The best of speakers explained the four ways of answering questions,
for the sake of training his disciples in debate and regarding the fourfold set of positions.
There are four types of questions: those requiring a categorical answer, those requiring an analytical answer, those requiring a counter-question, and those that are to be set aside;
as in the cases of death, birth, excellence, life, and the difference between substances.
One is designated as "proponent of the locus" (sthānavāditva), another is called "conceptual construction" (parikalpa);
another is known as "the path" (pratipad), and another is designated as "proponent of knowledge" (jñānavāditva). [295]
One who exists with pride, aversion, and attachment that have not abandoned their activity,
and for whom these have arisen and are not yet abandoned, is bound to that object.

The continuum of the aggregates is conjoined with these non-arisen mental factors, as well as with all others belonging to their own time-period; likewise, it is conjoined everywhere with those that have not yet arisen and with the remaining ones.
In this context, only two [of the three natures] are established as real, while the third exists only figuratively;
for it is grasped by those who stand in the middle because its cause consists of both the existent and the non-existent.
"All exists," "there is a partial existence," "all does not exist," and another,
"the proponent of the indeterminate existence"— these are remembered as the four proponents.
Among these, the first disputant possesses genuine excellence;
the others, however, are merely proud of their logic, being excluded from both reason and scripture.
Because he maintains the existence of the three time periods and the three constants by virtue of their functional efficacy, the first fourfold school is therefore called Sarvāstivāda. [301]

There are two known as the proponents of the alteration of entities (bhāvānyathika) and the alteration of states (avasthānyathika); another is the proponent of the alteration of otherness (anyathānyathika), while the third is the proponent of reasoning (yuktivādin). [302]
He maintains that the distinction between the time-periods is established by their activity (*kāritra*):
while performing that activity, it is the present time-period; once performed, it is the past; and when not yet performed, it is the other (the future). [303]
That sign which is perceived by the intellect is to be known as fourfold:
from the perspective of ultimate reality, from the perspective of conventional reality, from both, and also from the perspective of relativity. [304]
The past and the unarisen exist, because they are spoken of by the Buddha just like the present;
and because they are not objects of cognition, their existence is like that of the present.
Cognition does not have a non-existent object as its basis, whether according to scripture or through reasoning;
furthermore, the negation of a relation between a horse and a horn occurs only in dependence upon something else.
When a real entity such as form has perished, a cognition arises;
that cognition takes the aspect of the non-existence of the object, just like the mind of the Teacher regarding other things.
Because it serves as the basis for the arising of joy, fear, agitation, and the emergence of memory,
the capacity of the whole is manifested, just like the form of a jar illuminated by a lamp. [308]

Because the agent of the act of producing (*janīhākartṛ*) is already existent, like the five modes of being (*pañcabhāvavikāra*), it is observed to be a subordinate factor (*kriyāṅga*) to the action; therefore, it is an object that is modified (*vikārya*), like an object that is reached (*prāpyakarma*). [309]
A second birth is not possible for an entity that has already been born.
Because of the absence of qualities, secondary existence does not exist where primary existence is absent. [310]
When there is a similarity of properties, the application of that [term] is like sweet speech;
the manifestation of the primary gender is accepted as being like a child and so forth. [311]
The sky might bloom with sky-flowers, and a frog might grow a mane,
if intrinsic nature were to arise after having previously not existed through the power of mental cultivation.

O gentle one, tell me: how can a thing, whose dharmas are devoid of the power of stability and are accompanied by destruction and arising, attain the status of a real entity through dependent origination? [313]
In the world, mutual benefit is observed only between two existing things;
likewise, harm also occurs only between such, and not between a horse's horn and a snake's foot. [314]
That which is dependently originated does not exist by way of intrinsic nature;
that which does not exist by way of intrinsic nature exists as something other than that.
Causes merely bring about the state of an existing thing;
ministers can only exercise kingship over a prince who already possesses the nature of a king. [316]
When there is a collection of phenomena, efficacy arises, just as it does for accumulated atoms in the perception of a self. [317]
For one who holds that past karma is non-existent and that a future fruit is produced from what is non-existent,
it is clear that a son of a barren woman is born from an intermediate being.
Because it lacks the characteristics of a real entity and because its status as a substantial reality is not established,
that which is future or past does not possess the nature of a conceptual reality.
What is the obstacle? It is the deficiency of limbs; that is not because of the eternal existence of all things.
Therefore, listen from the virtuous: the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is indeed difficult to understand. [320]

The projection of a fruit by that which has acquired its capacity—due to its occurrence in the present time-path and its grasping of the constituent parts of the causal complex—is designated as "activity" (kāritra). [321]
Form does not possess the state of being present, nor does it possess the state of being past or future;
therefore, the self-identity of form is not held to undergo alteration through its movement across the time-periods (adhvan). [322]
A certain state arises for an existing entity;
likewise there is power, likewise time, likewise existence, and likewise action. [323]
The world is pervaded by conceptual constructions that delight the minds of the foolish;
however, that conceptual construction which grasps the mind with dualistic views is difficult to find.
One who is bound by other universal [defilements] remains so even when the vision of suffering has been abandoned;
likewise, even when a previous category has been abandoned, one remains bound by the remaining [defilements] that take that as their object.
The phenomena to be known are sixteenfold, each consisting of the three realms of existence; likewise, the factors are fivefold, as are the stainless ones and the consciousnesses. [326]
One should observe the elements, the sense-bases, and the truths, as well as their various modes,
impelled by the knowledge of the comprehension of phenomena and the knowledge of the underlying tendencies.

Those [factors] belonging to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its causes, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation, are the objects of the mind; they consist of three of their own [realms], one of the form realm, and the stainless [unconditioned].
Those born of form have as their objects three of their own level, one lower, and one upper, as well as the pure [dharmas].
Those pertaining to the formless realm have as their objects those belonging to the three realms, the threefold [categories], and the pure [dharmas].
All are to be known as superior to themselves; they possess equal departure, vision, and destruction [of defilements];
they are free from afflictions, have attained the three realms of existence, and have as their final sphere of activity the stainless [state].
That which belongs to the desire realm has the five objects as its sphere; that which belongs to the form realm has eight objects as its range;
that which belongs to the formless realm has ten objects as its range; and the pure [uncontaminated] has ten objects as its range for those very same ten.
Regarding the objects of the higher realms within the consciousnesses pertaining to the desire realm, three types of latent dispositions belonging to their own level—
those to be abandoned by cultivation, those that are omnipresent, and those of the form realm— adhere as latent tendencies.

Four [defilements] are abandoned through the revolution of their own stage; furthermore, three belonging to the realm of form, along with all those belonging to the formless realm, are abandoned through cultivation.
In exactly the same way, they also increase in relation to the second and likewise the fifth;
those with outflowing objects increase in relation to their own level and also in the third.
But when there is a transformation, those belonging to the desire realm have conditioned objects as their support;
the remainder is to be explained as before, and in the fourth [dhyāna] it is like the third.
But when [the spheres] are reversed, the four belonging to the desire realm are as before, except for the first;
in the first [sphere] belonging to the form realm, there are three below, and indeed three in its own [level].

The formless [attainments] are all-pervading, together with those abandoned through the path of cultivation; upon the revolution [of the basis], three belong to the lower realms and four belong to their own realm.
The four classes of beings belonging to the formless realm possess latent dispositions;
it is exactly the same in the second [dhyāna], and likewise in the fifth.
Those with outflows (sāsrava) that have their own realm as an object, as well as those belonging to the third [realm], also reside there;
however, when transformed, those pertaining to the form realm (rūpāpta) take conditioned phenomena as their objects.
But the rest should be understood as before; in the fourth [dhyāna] it is like the third.
One should understand that when the first formless [attainment] has undergone transformation, it is like the third.
Three belong to the desire realm; three belong to the form realm;
and likewise for the third and fifth, there are three each, as in the case of the form realm, when the transformation has occurred.

Furthermore, in the third [transformation], when one's own [basis] has undergone revolution, those that have their objects within one's own realm and are associated with outflows (sāsrava) become those that have their objects within one's own realm and are associated with the conditioned (saṃskṛta).

Up to the point of "otherness" (anyatva) and so forth, it should be explained in the fourth [case] just as in the third; however, when consciousness has undergone transformation, the wise one should designate it just as in the first.
The category to be abandoned by the path of cultivation, together with the omnipresent [defilements], lies latent in two realms; those belonging to the formless realm lie latent in the eye-faculty.
The three classes of phenomena pertaining to the desire realm and the form realm, which fall within the range of the visual faculty,
are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, by the vision of its cause, and by cultivation— three for each.
The formless [defilements] are to be abandoned by cultivation, and the universal [defilements] underlie them;
however, when there is a transformation [of the basis], four [remain], excluding those associated with equanimity and those to be abandoned by insight.
Regarding the faculty of suffering, however, that which belongs to the desire realm increases along with its own [factors] and the universal ones;
but as for the consciousness that has that as its object, the categories [of defilements] increase therein.
The three types of form-realm [defilements] are abandoned through universal [objects], cultivation, and destruction; however,
when another [realm] has arisen, the four [types] belonging to the desire realm continue to underlie as latent dispositions.

From the final existence in the realm of form (rūpabhava), all three universal proclivities (sarvagā) to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanāheya) persist; furthermore, four persist due to the non-turning away from the two [realms]. [349]
In the faculty of pleasure, in the mind that has it as its object, and also in the sphere of its activity,
the proclivities belonging to the desire realm and so forth, as well as those that are omnipresent, lie latent according to their respective conditions.
But all [factors] subsumed within the three realms are included in the mind-faculty;
when consciousness takes them as its object, they have all conditioned phenomena as their domain.
Only those [defilements] that have conditioned phenomena as their object persist after the transformation;
there is no distinction whatsoever here regarding the twofold transformation.

From a mind of one who possesses desire that is to be abandoned by seeing suffering and so forth, six minds may arise immediately thereafter; for such a person, five or five [minds] may arise subsequently.
One should specify the minds of one born in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) as being either one, five, six, seven, or ten. [354]
One should characterize these minds of one born in the formless realm as being fivefold belonging to their own realm; at the time of death, they are tenfold from the other [lower realms].
Because it acts as an associate and because it lies latent within, the mind is considered to be "with proclivities" (sānuśaya);
it is designated in two ways—as defiled and non-defiled—or in one way alone.

From delusion arises the view of a self-identity; from that, the view of grasping at extremes; from that, doubt and false views; from those, attachment to rules and observances; and from that, attachment to [wrong] views. [357]

Attachment and pride extend toward one's own [object], while hatred extends toward others; this sequence of theirs should be understood as such because of the predominance of their respective functions. [358]
However, due to association with good or bad friends, there is considered to be no fixed rule regarding its activity;
some affliction arises when all three causes are complete. [359]
The second quarter of the fifth chapter in the *Abhidharmadīpa-vibhāṣāprabhā-vṛtti*.

The third quarter of the fifth chapter: All afflictions (*kleśa*) except for ignorance (*avidyā*) in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) are considered the outflow of desire (*kāmāsrava*); excluding sloth (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*), those in the higher realms are the outflow of existence (*bhavāsrava*) because they are similar [in nature]. [360]
But that which is called ignorance is the root; thus it is ignorance pertaining to all realms.
Likewise, the floods and yokes exclude the [wrong] views, whereas they are treated separately due to their distinctiveness.
That ignorance constitutes two types of clinging as previously stated;
however, two consist of views.
All four together constitute one, because they rely upon the wrong path and so forth. [362]

The remaining [defilements] belong to the three realms; however, the last two arise along with the personal existence (ātmabhāva). Furthermore, they are shown to be fivefold by means of terms such as "fetter" (saṃyojana) and so forth.

In this [system], there are nine fetters (*saṃyojana*): envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*), as well as the two fetters of views (*dṛṣṭi*), because of the commonality of their being objects of intolerance and their nature as views. [364]
The remaining five latent tendencies are again of five kinds each;
he declared them as those conducive to the lower realm and those conducive to the higher realm.
The first and last two views constitute doubt;
sensual desire is twofold.
Through these two, there is no transcendence of the realm of desire. Furthermore, [the fetters] are nine.
The vehicle is established by means of three.
Because it is stated that there are two and one effects to be abandoned by vision, and because they are grasped by way of being abandoned by vision,
these three are thus illustrated, even though they all share the quality of being abandonable by vision.
Because they are the cause of all misfortune, because they act as adversaries to the Path,
and because they are devoid of correct reasoning, the three fetters are taught.

The two types of attachment arising from the realms of form and formlessness, along with the three arising from pride and delusion—these constitute the three bonds because they adhere to the three sensations and because of their firmness. [369]
Because they are composed of two pairs, four treatises are proclaimed:
those called covetousness, as well as hatred, and likewise the two types of misapprehension.
The secondary afflictions (upakleśa) should be understood as those such as impetuosity (saṃrambha) and so forth as previously described;
or alternatively, all afflicted mental factors designated as the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha).
The other root afflictions and impurities are designated as the six secondary afflictions.
Deceit, enmity, spite, guile, intoxication, and harmfulness.
Envy, jealousy, lack of shame, lack of dread, sloth, torpor, restlessness, anger, avarice, and bad conduct—these are the ten types of envelopments (*paryavasthāna*). [373]
From these [three roots], shamelessness, restlessness, and so forth arise as their non-concordant outflows;
while hypocrisy, lack of moral dread, torpor, drowsiness, and so forth arise from delusion.
Regret arises from doubt; anger and the like originate from hatred; while negligence, arrogance, malice, deceit, guile, and dissimulation arise from delusion. [375]
Furthermore, bodily rigidity and the like should be understood as arising from a mixture [of causes].
Malice is the outflow of the adherence to views; deceitfulness is the outflow of views.
The association of attachment with mental joy and pleasure is proclaimed; likewise, that of aversion with mental grief and pain. [377]
Delusion is associated with all [mental factors], while false view is associated with two mental factors; doubt is associated with dejection,
and the remaining [afflictions] are associated with gladness.
However, this rule applies to all those belonging to the desire realm by virtue of equanimity;
but for those born in other realms, [the abandonment occurs] through their own [factors] at each successive level.
Of envy, mental distress, remorse, and likewise of anger;
And likewise from being bitten, from being bound, and from injury.
Avarice, dejection, and mental gladness each arise with respect to something; likewise, deceit, guile, concealment, and torpor arise with both. [381]
Intoxication (mada), however, is associated with the aggregates of mind (sumanas) and pleasure (sukha); likewise are lack of shame (āhrīkya) and lack of dread (anapatrāpya).
And in the case of lethargy and restlessness, they are associated with five [mental factors].
Lack of shame, lack of dread, torpor and drowsiness, and likewise restlessness; [383]
......... [In the Abhidharmadīpa, in the commentary known as the Vibhāṣāprabhā, this is the third quarter of the fifth chapter.]
...[The fifth chapter is completed. ...
